title: Kodak Once Kept a Special Nuclear Device in Its Basement
summary:
For about 30 years, the camera and film company Eastman Kodak kept an unusual machine in a secure basement in Rochester, New York. It was a nuclear device about the size of a refrigerator, and it was used for research.

Kodak turned the device on in 1975. It was the country's first californium neutron flux multiplier, or CFX. Its job was to make a steady stream of neutrons, tiny particles found in the centers of atoms.

Kodak used the neutrons in two ways. First, it could test chemicals to find out exactly what was in them. Second, it could make neutron images, which work a bit like X-rays. X-rays have trouble showing light materials like water or film, but neutrons can show them. Put simply, if an X-ray shows you the crack in a pipe, neutrons will show you the leak.

The machine started with a tiny amount of a lab-made material, californium-252, which gives off neutrons on its own. Because californium is very expensive, its neutrons were sent through 52 plates of highly enriched uranium. When neutrons hit uranium atoms, some atoms split and released more neutrons. This made the stream up to 30 times stronger.

That might sound like a nuclear reactor, but there was a key difference. The CFX was designed so it could not keep a chain reaction going by itself. Without the californium, the process would fade out.

The device ran until 2006 behind walls two feet thick, under government security rules. Kodak and officials said it was tightly controlled. When it was taken apart, the uranium plates were carefully moved to a government facility. When news of the machine spread in 2012, many people were alarmed, but the real story is a clever piece of Cold War engineering.
why_it_matters: The story shows how nuclear science has been used as a research tool, and why careful safety rules matter when handling powerful materials.

background_read: Atoms have a center called a nucleus, made of protons and neutrons.
In heavy elements like uranium, a nucleus can split when hit by a neutron, releasing energy and more neutrons; this splitting is called fission.
If each split causes enough new splits, a chain reaction keeps going, which is how nuclear reactors work.
Scientists also use neutrons as a tool to see inside materials and find out what they are made of.
